title: Handling pushback from instructors when restructuring their workload

action: I met with them one-on-one before announcing anything team-wide, and listened first. Their concern about quality was legitimate, not just self-interest. I shared the utilization data openly so we were looking at the same facts, and invited them to help redesign the schedule instead of handing them a finished plan. We moved TAs onto lab support so instructors could focus on teaching, and we built in a check: if apprentice checkpoint scores dropped, we'd revisit [confirm: the actual compromise].
result: The instructor became a supporter of the new model [confirm], the program saved $72,000 over two years, and 93% of apprentices still moved on to Amazon on-the-job training. What I learned: people resist changes done to them far more than changes they help shape, and a shared quality check turns a cost discussion into a common goal.

title: Choosing an explainable scoring model over ML for incident triage
relatedProject: Change Radar (portfolio project)
situation: I built Change Radar, a portfolio project inspired by my eBay work. It answers the first question in any incident: what changed right before this alert? Change history was split across three systems (change requests, deploys and feature flags), and the tool had to rank which recent change most likely caused a given alert.
task: Design a ranking that an on-call engineer would trust within seconds, that works without labeled incident history, and that I could verify was correct.
action: I rejected a learned model: I had no labeled incidents to train on, and an engineer under pressure needs to be able to check the ranking. Instead I multiplied four factors that are easy to explain: time proximity (halving every 15 minutes before the alert, with a 5-minute allowance for clock skew), blast radius (dependency hops found by a breadth-first search over the service catalog, with cycle handling), change type and declared risk. Every score comes with plain-English reasons such as 'ads-serving depends on ads-bidder'. I deliberately kept missing metadata out of the score, because an undocumented change isn't more likely to be the cause, just harder to investigate. To prove the ranking worked, I generated demo data with three planted incidents, each with one real cause and decoys (an unrelated deploy 3 minutes before the alert, a same-service deploy 48 minutes before), and wrote tests asserting the real cause ranks first.
result: All three planted incidents rank their real cause #1, checked by unit tests at several start times and by an end-to-end test against Elasticsearch, with correlation queries returning in tens of milliseconds. The written reasons make the ranking easy to check and argue with. What I learned: in tools for people under pressure, being able to explain a result beats a marginally better one, and planting known answers in test data is the best way to show an algorithm works.

title: Building fault-tolerant, idempotent ingestion across three different source APIs
relatedProject: Change Radar (portfolio project)
situation: Change Radar pulls change records from three source systems that each behave differently. ServiceNow uses offset/limit paging and 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss' UTC timestamps. The deploy API uses 1-based pages and ISO-8601 times. The feature-flag log uses 0-based pages, epoch-millisecond timestamps and a hasMore flag. Real integrations look like this, and they also fail independently.
task: Ingest all three into one Elasticsearch index reliably: no duplicates on re-runs, no single source able to block the others, and failures visible to operators.
action: I gave each source a small adapter that hides its paging and returns raw records, each of which knows how to normalize itself into one ChangeEvent shape. Rather than one Spring Batch job with three steps, I ran one job per source, so a ServiceNow outage can't stop deploys from being indexed, and each source reports its own status, counts and error at /api/ingest/status. Document ids are source:externalId, so re-ingesting overwrites instead of duplicating. The processor drops non-production deploys and records missing metadata at the same step. I tested the full pipeline with Testcontainers against a real Elasticsearch 9 instance, including a test that re-running ingestion leaves the document count unchanged.
result: All 271 demo changes across the three sources are ingested on a 60-second schedule. Staging deploys are filtered out (27 skipped), re-runs are proven idempotent, and the backend's 32 tests run in CI on every push. What I learned: designing for partial failure and safe re-runs up front is far cheaper than debugging duplicate data in production. It was the same lesson as my eBay Spring Batch work, applied from day one.

title: Shipping a backend-heavy project as a zero-cost live demo
relatedProject: Change Radar (portfolio project)
situation: Change Radar needs Elasticsearch and a Spring Boot backend, but a portfolio project only matters if a recruiter can click a link and see it work. Hosting the full stack 24/7 would cost money, and asking a reviewer to run docker compose loses most of them.
task: Give the project a live, free demo on GitHub Pages without faking its behavior or maintaining two versions of the logic that could drift apart.
action: I put the frontend behind an API interface with two implementations: an HTTP client for the real backend, and a demo client that loads a snapshot exported from a real backend run and answers the same calls in the browser. The demo shifts every timestamp by the time since export, so the incidents always look recent. Correlation in the demo needs a TypeScript copy of the Java scorer, which is a real drift risk. I handled it with a shared file of scoring test cases that both the JUnit and Vitest suites must pass, so any formula change that isn't made in both places fails CI. A GitHub Actions workflow builds the demo variant under the repo's base path and deploys it, and a separate CI workflow runs both test suites.
result: The project has a free live demo that behaves like the real one (the same culprit ranks first with the same score), it works on mobile, and the two scorers are guaranteed to match by 9 shared test cases. What I learned: think about how a reviewer will actually reach your work, and when duplication is unavoidable, make tests enforce that the copies agree.

title: Designing a supervisor-based multi-agent research framework with Google ADK and MCP
relatedProject: CityU AI Hub - Multi-Agent Research Framework

title: Securing API routes with JWT and Auth0 during a CodeDay Labs internship

title: Handling a rate-limited upstream API without losing data
relatedProject: eBay Ads - Control Center change metadata
situation: The experiment-change job called the internal experimentation platform's API to enrich every change with details: placements, sites, traffic and history. In April 2022 the job started getting HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) responses. The platform was rate-limiting us, and enrichment calls were failing, so experiment data was missing from Control Center during those periods.
task: Stay within the platform's limits without permanently losing the experiment changes that the failed calls should have captured.
action: Once I traced the failures to 429s, I cut the number of calls the job made per run and spread them out over longer intervals, so we stopped hitting the limit. Calling less often risked leaving gaps, so I made sure the job backfilled the periods it had missed, and I backfilled the experiment data lost while we were being throttled. This built on an earlier change I'd made so that the job reported success even when a downstream API returned a 500 error, meaning one flaky dependency couldn't fail a whole run.
result: The 429s stopped, the gaps in experiment data were backfilled, and the job ran within the platform's limits from then on. What I learned: treat an upstream API's limits as part of your design. The fix is to call less often, and backfilling is what makes calling less often safe.

title: When my bug broke production ingestion, and a senior engineer took the blame with me
relatedProject: eBay Ads - Control Center change metadata
situation: In October 2021, a couple of months into the job, I shipped a change to the change-ingestion batch job with a rookie mistake: an unhandled null from an upstream metadata endpoint caused a NullPointerException. An analyst on our team noticed that change data had stopped appearing in Control Center, the very data on-call engineers relied on to diagnose revenue drops.
task: Restore ingestion quickly, repair any bad data, and make sure this kind of failure couldn't silently stop the pipeline again.
action: I found the null that caused the NullPointerException and fixed it. While investigating, I also found that a placement-ID regex was capturing digit sequences from other IDs and from dates. I fixed the regex, added unit tests for it, and deployed both fixes the same day. Then I corrected the bad placement data in production for the 5 experiments affected between October 11 and 22. When it came up with the team, the senior engineer who had reviewed my code immediately said he was accountable too, without being asked. I took that as the standard to live up to, and I added guardrails: null checks and try/catch around calls to external data, so one bad record or endpoint is logged and skipped instead of stopping the whole job.
result: Ingestion was restored and the data repaired within days, and the guardrails meant later upstream problems degraded gracefully instead of stopping ingestion. I also took away how good teams handle mistakes: the reviewer sharing accountability made it safe to report problems fast, and I've tried to do the same since. What I learned: write defensive code wherever external data comes in, test the parsing code, and fix the culture along with the code.

title: Cutting the time to link a revenue drop to its cause from hours to minutes
relatedProject: eBay Ads - Control Center change metadata
situation: I was a Software Engineer II on eBay's Ads Infra team, which ran Control Center, the internal portal where the ads organization monitored revenue, clicks and impressions and handled alerts. When a revenue or metric drop alerted, on-call engineers had to work out which change caused it: an A/B experiment ramping up, a code deploy, a merchandising front-end config change, a data-warehouse change or a streaming job update. That information was scattered across ServiceNow, the experimentation platform and other tools, and the experimentation platform's own UI had no way to connect a site-impacting metric drop to an experiment change. Linking a drop to a change could take hours.
task: I owned everything related to change data. The goal was to bring every relevant change into Control Center so that whoever was investigating a drop could see what changed, when, and what it affected, right next to the metric.
action: I built Spring Batch jobs, one per change source, that pulled from each system's API. Experiments came from ServiceNow change requests, enriched with details from the experimentation platform's API (placements, sites, business units, traffic served, start and duration). Front-end config changes, code rollouts and rollbacks, data-warehouse changes and streaming job operations came from their own sources. Each job normalized the records into one change model and indexed it in Elasticsearch. Some sources had no change history, so for those the jobs took hourly snapshots and stored the differences between snapshots as change events. On the front end, I built the Changes page in React: a searchable, sortable, filterable table, plus annotations on the time-series charts, so hovering over a point in a revenue chart showed the changes that took effect at that moment. Later, in 2023, I added ads-platform changes and planned experiments that hadn't launched yet, so teams could see upcoming changes as well as past ones. I also wrote the SOP for confirming whether an experiment's change was missing, and I became the named contact when one was.
result: My manager described the impact this way: correlating an issue with recent changes 'could take hours in some cases'; with the change information in Control Center, recent changes 'could be surfaced within 10 minutes, and sometimes within seconds depending on the polling cycle.' The tool served roughly 20 to 40 internal users across ads infrastructure, QA, experimentation, release management, merchandising front end, analytics, problem management and engineering management. Over about two years the pipeline grew from experiments alone to six or more change types, and checking recent changes in Control Center became a standard step in on-call investigations and incident write-ups. What I learned: during an incident, putting the right data in front of the person investigating does more than a smarter alert would.

title: Shipping the change-investigation UI one small release at a time
relatedProject: eBay Ads - Control Center change metadata
situation: Once change data was in Elasticsearch, the people investigating drops (on-call engineers, analysts and product managers) needed to find the relevant change fast. The first version of the Changes page was a bare list that was hard to search or narrow down during an incident.

I also standardized site names across the Core Metrics and Changes pages so filters matched, and I added hover annotations on time-series charts that showed which changes took effect at each point. result: The Changes page became the first stop in on-call investigations and was used by roughly 20 to 40 internal users: ads infra and QA engineers, the experimentation team, release management, the merchandising front-end team, analysts, problem managers and engineering managers. Shipping in small increments meant feedback reached production within days. What I learned: incident tools improve fastest through many small releases shaped by the people using them, and consistent naming, such as site names, matters more than it looks.

title: Evolving an Elasticsearch schema without reindexing, then migrating 14 months of data
relatedProject: eBay Ads - Control Center change metadata
situation: Change records in Elasticsearch needed structured fields such as placement IDs that could be searched. The existing 'data' field had been dynamically mapped as text early on. In Elasticsearch you can't change an existing field's type without reindexing, so a nested object couldn't go into that field. The indexes were also created per year, and each new year's index needed explicit date mappings, or time-range queries would break.
task: Add structured, searchable fields without disrupting a production index that the on-call team used every day, and later move the data into a cleaner v2 schema.
action: Rather than reindexing production for one field, I added a new, explicitly mapped object field (info.placementIds), updated the batch job to write it using XContentBuilder arrays and updated the UI to read and search it. I fixed the historical placement data in production for the affected experiments. I documented the yearly index-mapping step (explicit date types for start, end, effect-start and last-modified times) so new indexes wouldn't silently break queries, and I flattened the experiment change structure to remove duplicated fields. When we moved to a v2 change schema served by our metadata service, I migrated all the change data from June 2021 to July 2022 from the v1 index to v2.
result: Placement-based search shipped without a risky production reindex, the yearly index rollover became a documented step instead of a surprise, and the v2 migration finished in September 2022 with 14 months of history intact. What I learned: decide mappings explicitly from the start, because dynamic mapping is a shortcut that costs you later, and when production is in use, an additive change beats a perfect reindex.

title: Using sampled data to change a change-tracking policy I didn't own
relatedProject: eBay Ads - Control Center change metadata
situation: Ramping an A/B experiment's traffic up or down can move revenue as much as a code deploy, but at eBay only one ServiceNow change request (CR) was filed per experiment, when it was created. Every later ramp up or down was invisible to anyone looking for what changed. The policy belonged to the operations and problem-management team, not mine. An earlier attempt to file a CR per experiment change had been rolled back after it reportedly produced 40,000 change records a day, so the idea was widely seen as too noisy.
task: I worked on the ads infrastructure team as a contractor, with no authority over the policy. My task was to make the case for filing a CR on every experiment ramp up and down, and to make sure the change data we then ingested would be meaningful rather than noise.
action: I started by questioning the 40,000 figure. eBay doesn't ramp anywhere near 40,000 experiments a day, so that number pointed to a bug, not to the real volume. I sampled and tracked experiments over the course of a day to measure how often traffic actually changed, which came to about 30 changes a day. I brought that estimate, and the visibility gap it would close, to the problem-management team and the experimentation team, which turned 'this will flood ServiceNow' into a manageable, concrete number. On our side, I made sure the data we ingested deserved the attention: we deduplicated so each experiment change was counted once, and we filtered out changes that didn't affect anything, like text edits, content updates or process-step updates that had previously come through as 'changes'.
result: The policy changed. Multiple CRs per experiment ramp up and down went to production in March 2022, about three months after I started the discussion. Experiment traffic changes became visible in ServiceNow and in our change correlation, so on-call engineers could see a ramp-up that happened right before a drop. What I learned: when a proposal has been rejected because of a scary number, checking that number is often the whole argument, and filtering out noise is what makes more data worth having.

title: Interviewing new grads and turning tribal knowledge into SOPs

title: Building a metadata service to stop duplicate and double writes to Elasticsearch
relatedProject: eBay Ads - Control Center change metadata
situation: As the change pipeline grew, several batch jobs each wrote directly to Elasticsearch, each with its own client code and its own idea of a document. I found duplicate change records and double writes in the index, including a bug where converting ZonedDateTime values produced a second write. Meanwhile other teams wanted to add their own changes (product launches, for example), and the UI and email digests read the index with queries copied in several places.
task: Give the change data one owner: a single, consistent way to write and query changes that ruled out duplicates and that other teams and systems could use safely.
action: I built a new Spring Boot service with a write API and a query API in front of the change indexes, and moved the batch jobs from writing to Elasticsearch directly to calling the service. To make writes idempotent, I gave each change a unique, deterministic document ID and switched inserts to upserts, so re-running a job updated records instead of duplicating them. I fixed the ZonedDateTime double write and standardized epoch-time conversion in a shared library. I added error handling and unit tests on the POST API, built a client in our shared common library so every job called the service the same way, and wrote the API design doc. The query API supported time ranges, multiple change types, sites, business units and placement filters, which the UI then used.
result: The service went to production in May 2022, and by June all ingestion jobs wrote through it. Duplicates stopped because re-runs were now safe, and other teams could add their changes, such as search-team product launches, through the API instead of asking us. What I learned: once more than one writer touches the same data store, give it a single owner with idempotent writes. Duplicate data is much easier to prevent than to clean up.

title: On call when revenue data dropped to zero: triaging about 30 alerts down to one deploy
relatedProject: eBay Ads - Control Center change metadata
situation: On November 16, 2021, while I was on call for ads infrastructure, revenue alerts started firing early in the morning. Our real-time sales data in ClickHouse had stopped showing revenue after 2 AM PST, which set off nearly 30 P1 to P3 alerts at once: global revenue, mobile web revenue, GMV for every site (US, UK, DE, AU and more), and data-quality monitors. Any one of them could look like eBay was losing ads revenue.
task: Work out whether revenue was really falling or our data was broken, find the cause, get the right owners to fix it, and keep the alert noise from burying everything else.
action: Working from the alerts, I checked the underlying data and found the problem was the pipeline, not buyers: there was no revenue in ClickHouse after 2 AM across every site and platform, Seeing zeros was itself the anomaly, and nothing had happened (no major event, outage or launch) that could explain revenue really going to zero, so I treated it as an ingestion problem, not a business problem. I paged the on-call engineer for the team that owns the real-time sales ingestion, and snoozed the affected alerts for 12 hours while ClickHouse was affected so new, real alerts wouldn't be buried. The root cause was a code deploy to one of their real-time ingestion services just before 2 AM, which was inserting records with eventWeek=0 and broke the revenue queries. The deploy was rolled back, the data caught up, and the missing 2 AM to 12 PM window was backfilled. I wrote the initial RCA for our team.
result: The deploy was rolled back, data caught up, and the gap was backfilled, so no revenue was actually lost; it was a data problem. The honest lesson I wrote into the RCA was about me: the deploy had been visible in our own changes view, the tool I was building, and I hadn't checked it first. Checking recent changes became the first step in my on-call routine and in the checklist I maintained for the team. What I learned: when many alerts start at the same moment, suspect the shared data source before suspecting the business, and stop alert noise quickly so the team can think.

title: Reducing backend response time by 80% with async processing and caching
relatedProject: Worldwide American - Social Media Ranking Platform

title: Building the authentication layer for a microservices platform

I responded by [confirm: e.g., consolidating services, adding Docker Compose for local dev, or documenting the service map], and I've since changed my approach: start with a modular monolith with clear internal boundaries, and split out a service only when there's a concrete scaling, ownership or deployment reason.

title: Architecting a Spring Cloud microservices platform from scratch
relatedProject: Worldwide American - Social Media Ranking Platform
situation: Worldwide American needed a social media ranking platform, and I was responsible for the full architecture as well as sourcing and onboarding the engineers who would build on it. The system had to support several core domains and growing traffic.
task: Design a backend that could scale and stay maintainable for a small, growing team, and get it into production on AWS.
action: I designed a Spring Cloud Netflix architecture with an API Gateway as the single entry point, a Composite Service to aggregate responses, separate Core Services per domain, a Discovery Server for service registration, a Config Server for centralized configuration and an Admin Server for monitoring. I used RabbitMQ (Spring Cloud Bus) to fan out configuration changes from the config repository to every service without redeploying. Each core service had its own AWS RDS MySQL instance, and I deployed everything to EC2. I built the authentication layer with Spring Security, set up Git, GitHub and JIRA workflows, and onboarded new engineers on the architecture.
result: The platform launched with services that could be deployed independently, live config updates and a consistent security layer, and new engineers could ramp up on clear service boundaries. Combined with the async and caching work, backend response time improved by 80%. Looking back, I'd weigh the operational overhead of this many services against the team's size more carefully. That tradeoff is worth bringing up in a system design interview.
